title: **Title:** range_sortna(): docs say `decreasing = TRUE` is unsupported, but it appears to work
description:
**Package version:** bit 4.6.0

### Summary

The documentation for `range_sortna()` says for `decreasing`: *"currently only FALSE is supported"*. However, passing `decreasing = TRUE` appears to work correctly: the unsortedness flag (4th element of the `range_sortna` attribute) checks for decreasing order instead of increasing order.

### Without NAs

```r
library(bit)

attr(range_sortna(c(2L, 1L, 0L), decreasing = FALSE), "range_sortna")
#> [1] 0 2 0 1

attr(range_sortna(c(2L, 1L, 0L), decreasing = TRUE), "range_sortna")
#> [1] 0 2 0 0

attr(range_sortna(c(0L, 1L, 2L), decreasing = FALSE), "range_sortna")
#> [1] 0 2 0 0

attr(range_sortna(c(0L, 1L, 2L), decreasing = TRUE), "range_sortna")
#> [1] 0 2 0 1
```

A decreasing vector is flagged as sorted (0) only with `decreasing = TRUE`, and an increasing vector is flagged as unsorted (1) with `decreasing = TRUE`.

### With NAs and each `na.last` setting

```r
attr(range_sortna(c(2L, NA, 1L, 0L), decreasing = TRUE), "range_sortna")
#> [1] 0 2 0 0

attr(range_sortna(c(2L, NA, 1L, 0L), decreasing = TRUE, na.last = TRUE), "range_sortna")
#> [1] 0 2 1 0

attr(range_sortna(c(2L, NA, 1L, 0L), decreasing = TRUE, na.last = FALSE), "range_sortna")
#> [1] 0 2 1 0
```

This also appears to work correctly with NAs: in all three cases the non-NA values `2 1 0` are flagged as sorted in decreasing order (4th element is 0).

### Question

Is `decreasing = TRUE` intended to be supported? If so, the documentation could be updated to reflect this. If not (e.g. if there are known cases where it gives wrong results), perhaps the function should raise an error or warning rather than silently accepting the argument.

title: `shellsort()`, `shellorder()`, and `shellsortorder()` crash the R session on a zero-length `integer64` vector
description:
### Reproducible example

```r
library(bit64)
library(bit)

empty_vec <- bit64::integer64(0)
bit::shellsort(empty_vec)
# R session crashes

keys <- bit64::as.integer64(numeric(0))
pos  <- integer(0)
bit::shellorder(keys, pos)
# R session crashes

bit::shellsortorder(keys, pos)
# R session crashes
```

Each line crashes the R session (fatal error, session terminates) when run on its own - no R-level error or warning, just an immediate crash. Confirmed on all three functions individually.

### Expected behavior

A zero-length input should return `0L` (no NAs found) without modifying the empty vector, similar to how `sort(bit64::integer64(0))` handles it cleanly. Non-empty vectors, including ones with `NA`s, work correctly.

### Environment


R version: 4.5.3
Platform: Windows
bit version: 4.6.0
bit64 version: 4.6.0.1

title: `chunk` fails if package "ff" is loaded (instead of absent or attached)
description:
`bit::chunk` fails if package "ff" is loaded; it works fine if package "ff" is attached or not loaded.

`utils::packageVersion("bit")` # 4.0.4
code used by `bit:::chunk.default` to check for "ff": `"ff" %in% loadedNamespaces()`

#### Example 1: `bit::chunk` works if "ff" is not loaded (and not attached)
```
"ff" %in% loadedNamespaces() # FALSE
exists(".rambytes") # FALSE

bit::chunk(1) # chunk.default uses else clause
$`1:1`
range index (ri) from 1 to 1 maxindex 1
```

#### Example 2: `bit::chunk` fails if "ff" is loaded (and not attached)
```
requireNamespace("ff")
"ff" %in% loadedNamespaces() # TRUE
exists(".rambytes") # FALSE

bit::chunk(1)
Error in get(".rambytes") : object '.rambytes' not found
```


#### Example 3: `bit::chunk` works if "ff" is attached
```
library("ff")
"ff" %in% loadedNamespaces() # TRUE
exists(".rambytes") # TRUE

bit::chunk(1)
$`1:1`
range index (ri) from 1 to 1 maxindex 1
```

----
#### Possible solutions (among others) may include
- update `chunk.default` to test for existence of `.rambytes` (on the search path) directly instead of querying whether "ff" is loaded
```
RECORDBYTES <- if (exists(".rambytes")) ## replacing `if ("ff" %in% loadedNamespaces())`
  get(".rambytes")[get("vmode")(x)]
else c(raw = 1L, character = 4L, logical = 4L, integer = 4L,
  double = 8L, complex = 16L)[typeof(x)]
}
```
- or maybe something with `getExportedValue("ff", ".rambytes")` to load "ff" and extract ".rambytes" (given package "ff" is installed)?

Thanks!

title: `void R_bit_set_attr(...)` needs a different prototype
description:
Found while working on sanitizer CI for `data.table`:

```
dotcode.c:760:11: runtime error: call to function R_bit_set_attr through pointer to incorrect function type 'struct SEXPREC *(*)(struct SEXPREC *, struct SEXPREC *, struct SEXPREC *)'
/tmp/RtmpB1L8Jt/R.INSTALL10a075341d7f/bit/src/attrutil.c:5: note: R_bit_set_attr defined here
SUMMARY: UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer: undefined-behavior dotcode.c:760:11
```

Judging by `dotcode.c`, this must be R's own `.Call()` (e.g. [here](https://github.com/r-lib/bit/blob/c5ccbc0974761a58cb7d0ca2adc3d9280570b380/R/attrutil.R#L125)) running `void R_bit_set_attr(SEXP x, SEXP which, SEXP value)`:
https://github.com/r-lib/bit/blob/c5ccbc0974761a58cb7d0ca2adc3d9280570b380/src/attrutil.c#L4

Unlike with `.C`, functions that are called by `.Call` must return a `SEXP`, not `void`: https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Calling-_002eCall
https://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Registering-native-routines

Since the R callers always ignore the return value, it can be `x` or `R_NilValue` or something else, but it has to be there. Interesting that we've always been lucky that the `rax` register kept a valid `SEXP` pointer after the function call, so when R [used it](https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/blob/836c2a24ed118f99a546e8262faee3cf5a1aae4c/src/main/dotcode.c#L760) as the [return value](https://github.com/r-devel/r-svn/blob/836c2a24ed118f99a546e8262faee3cf5a1aae4c/src/main/dotcode.c#L1402), it didn't cause any problems.

title: Bug in `bit:::xor.logical` (drops matrix dimensions)
description:
When applied to a matrix, `bit:::xor.logical` drops matrix dimensions.  Since `base::xor` (and `bit:::xor.default`) retain matrix dimensions, this means that the results of `xor()` calls can differ depending on whether the `bit` package is loaded.

I've confirmed this for `bit 4.5.0` (the latest CRAN release) on `R 4.4.1` as per the reprex below.

``` r
library(bit)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'bit'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     xor

m <- matrix(TRUE)

xor(m, m)
#> [1] FALSE

bit:::xor.logical(m, m)
#> [1] FALSE

base::xor(m, m)
#>       [,1]
#> [1,] FALSE

bit:::xor.default(m, m)
#> default
#>       [,1]
#> [1,] FALSE
```

title: read/write bits
description:
Hello, Thank you for your efforts.  It is very fast.  I tried it on the PRIME sieve where the idx are the prime numbers.

For n=1000 primes, I overshoot using `gn = ceiling( n * log(n) + n * log(log(n)) )`

Here is the format of the output... I truncate the function result to exactly n = 1000, but keep the full calculation; in this case it looks like there are 1102 primes with `gn` as upper bound.

```
bitwhich: 1102/8841 occupying only 1102 int32 in 1 representation
    1     2     3     4     5     6     7     8        8834  8835  8836  8837  8838  8839  8840  8841 
FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE    .. FALSE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE 
 ```
My question is about storage.  From my understanding, if I just save/load or saveRDS/readRDS on the 8841 elements, the filesize should only be about 1.1KB ... Trying both methods (save/saveRDS), I get 2.6KB ... it throws an error when I try writeBin.
